title: ASK THE BEACH — The Commons Science Fair
dek: Every booth proves one thing in public.
body:
Most science fairs ask how to judge a project. Ask the Beach begins one step earlier: why would half the beach wander in, touch something, bring a friend, return at sunset, and talk about it tomorrow?

Popularity is not a marketing layer. It is a scientific design constraint. The phenomenon must be visible from the path. A visitor must become useful within ninety seconds. A result must change in public. The question must belong to the place. Excellence must have more than one shape. Children and adults should need one another. The day needs an ending worth staying for. And next season needs a public proof it can reproduce, improve, or overturn.

The imagined Commons Science Fair has seven color-coded avenues—sun, wind, water, sand, sound, life, and materials—and twelve small experiments. Shadow Atlas compares shade geometry and comfort. Wind Fingerprints turns contained motion into paper patterns. Tabletop Tide uses closed freshwater models to compare miniature edges without touching the ocean or pretending to certify coastal engineering. Angle of Repose keeps clean brought aggregate in contained trays. Cup Choir makes low-volume sound tactile. Living Atlas makes repeated observation valuable without collecting nature. Salt-Air Library, Pack-Down Physics, and Best Failure ask what deserves to return next season.

Every booth follows one recipe: a testable question, a visible ninety-second hook, one voluntary visitor move, an accumulating public measure, and one useful local takeaway. Nobody is assigned a shared role. The route builder asks why a visitor came—touch, build, help the coast, compete, bring everyone, find beauty, or stay late—and returns a 15-, 45-, or 120-minute route entirely in the browser.

Competition has two layers. The one-hundred-point project score respects question, method, evidence, imagination, and public explanation. Six sculptural public awards notice Best Explanation, Most Borrowable, Best Failure, Smallest Big Effect, Most Useful, and Audience Keeps. Public applause does not replace evidence, and a failed result can receive the day's most serious attention.

The fair opens through a curiosity gate, runs two public test rounds with a method swap between them, gathers for a proof walk, and ends at blue hour. Seven avenues converge on one low results theater. The public proof records the exact question, method, repeated result, contradiction, unknown, safely repeatable move, and clean-return receipt. Then every booth packs home.

Ask the Beach is an unofficial PointCast editorial rehearsal. It announces no event, permit, school program, competition, registration, experiment, public data collection, partnership, contribution, installation, vendor activity, citizen-science project, or physical gathering. An actual organized Dockweiler setup begins with current Los Angeles County requirements, qualified review, site conditions, access, supervision, insurance, and a specific safety plan.

media.alt: An intergenerational science fair enters seven colorful avenues through a reversible curiosity gate beside the beach.
